meta.blurb: A fifteenth-century monk writes by candlelight in a stone cell, and his plain advice is still read after more than five hundred years. Thomas a Kempis, in this Christian classic, speaks of humility, inner peace and patience, and of friendship with Christ.
meta.bible: Thomas à Kempis: a monk and writer born about 1380 in Kempen, in the Holy Roman Empire, who spent most of his life at Mount Saint Agnes, a monastery near Zwolle in the Netherlands; he died in 1471; the work is traditionally credited to him. The Imitation of Christ: a Christian devotional book written in Latin in the early fifteenth century, in four short books. Book One: advice for the spiritual life. Book Two: advice for the inner life. Book Three: a conversation between Christ and a disciple on inward comfort. Book Four: an invitation to Holy Communion. Christ: Jesus of Nazareth, the centre of the Christian faith. Gospel: the Christian account of the life of Jesus; the book quotes the Gospels of Luke and Matthew. Psalms: the sacred songs of the Bible. Scriptures: the Christian Bible. Latin: the language of the original. Netherlands and Dutch: where Thomas lived. Zwolle: a town near his monastery. Holy Communion: the sacred meal that many Christians share. Voice and tone: reverent, gentle and clear; every beat says which part of the book it comes from; teachings are attributed to Thomas and to the Christian tradition; the text is respectful to readers of any background and never urges one tradition above another; paraphrase, never long quotation.

beats.scene: Four small books lie in a stack on a wooden table
beats.summary: The work has four short books, and it asks the reader to follow Christ by changing the heart.

beats.summary: Knowledge without humility has little worth, and a humble farmer is better than a proud scholar.

beats.summary: Thomas warns against thinking too highly of oneself and invites readers to see themselves honestly.

beats.summary: Thomas advises reading the Scriptures for their truth and benefit, not for fine language.

beats.summary: Disordered desires leave the heart restless, and peace begins when we master our wants.

beats.summary: Thomas praises solitude and silence, and says people may make plans but only God decides the result.

beats.summary: Thomas urges readers to remember death and to live each day with care.

beats.scene: A man begins to sweep a stone floor early in the morning
beats.summary: Book One ends with a call to begin changing for the better today, with small steps.

beats.summary: Book Two begins: the kingdom of God is within, so turn the heart inward.

beats.scene: Two villagers shake hands under an old tree
beats.summary: First be at peace yourself, and then you will be able to bring peace to others.

beats.summary: Simplicity and purity are the two wings that lift a person above earthly things.

beats.summary: The royal road of the holy cross: hardship cannot be avoided, but it can be carried with patience and love.

beats.summary: Book Three is a conversation in which Christ speaks to the faithful soul within.

beats.scene: A student sits in a quiet room, ear tilted, lamp glowing
beats.summary: Truth teaches without noisy words, speaking quietly to the listening heart.

beats.scene: A runner leaps happily over a hill carrying a light bundle
beats.summary: The love of God makes every burden light and lifts the heart.

beats.scene: A traveller kneels by a bright door at the end of a long road
beats.summary: Thomas longs for closeness with God and asks the reader to approach in simple faith.

beats.summary: Taken together, the four books ask for a life that is humble, patient, inward and loving.

beats.summary: Over six centuries the book has been copied, printed and translated, and read by countless people.

B1B2: Thomas à Kempis was a monk who lived in the Netherlands in the fourteen hundreds. Tradition says that he wrote this small book of guidance in Latin for people who wanted a deeper life with God.
The book is made up of four short parts, and each one is a set of quiet chapters. It does not tell a story, but it speaks directly to the reader about the inner life.
In the first chapter of Book One, Thomas asks readers to follow Christ rather than only study him. Knowing many words about a good life, he says, is not the same as living one.
Thomas says that a humble farmer who serves God is better than a proud scholar who studies the stars. A person who is clever but has no humility, he says, is not truly wise.
Thomas warns readers not to think too highly of themselves, because everyone has faults. If we see ourselves honestly, he suggests, we will be less eager to judge anyone else.
Thomas reminds us that one day we will be asked what we did, not how much we read. So the best use of a book, he suggests, is to become a kinder and more honest person.
When we read the Scriptures, Thomas says, we should look for the truth rather than for fine style. The words should be read with the same simple spirit in which they were first written.
Thomas teaches that the heart becomes restless whenever it wants too much. Peace begins when we learn to control our desires instead of letting them control us.
Thomas warns that hope placed in friends, wealth or praise will sooner or later disappoint us. In his view, none of these things is strong enough to carry our whole weight.
Thomas notices that people often leave a long conversation less peaceful than when they began it. He advises us to speak less, and to keep our words for things that are useful and kind.
In the twelfth chapter, Thomas explains that trouble can be good for us. It reminds us that we are not in control, and it teaches us to be patient and humble.

Thomas teaches that no one in this life is completely free from temptation, not even the holy. The best time to resist, he says, is at the very beginning, when a wrong thought first knocks at the door.
It is easy to judge other people, Thomas says, because we do not know what lies in their hearts. He tells us to look at our own faults first, since they are the ones we can change.
Thomas points out that we cannot even make ourselves into the person we wish to be. How can we expect other people to become exactly as we would like them to be?
Thomas loves silence, because in a quiet place a person can hear what is happening inside. He also reminds us that people may make plans, but the final result is not ours to decide.
In the chapter on death, Thomas says that life is shorter than we think. He suggests that we should live each day with care, because we do not know when it will end.
The first book of Thomas ends with a clear call to begin at once, without any more delay. He does not want us to wait for a perfect day, but to take one small step toward a better life today.
Book Two begins with a line from the Gospels, that the kingdom of God is within you. Thomas takes this to mean that we should turn our attention inward and make a quiet home for God in our hearts.
Thomas says that a peaceful person does more good than a learned one. If you first make peace in your own heart, you can then bring peace to the people around you.
Thomas imagines that a person is lifted above the world by two wings, simplicity and purity. Simplicity belongs to the intention, he says, and purity belongs to the heart.
Thomas says that the joy of a good conscience is quiet but very strong. Praise from others is pleasant, yet it cannot make a person better than he truly is.
Thomas writes that Jesus should be loved above all things and above all people. A friend like this, he says, will stay with us when every other friend has gone.
Thomas notices that many people love Jesus while life is comfortable, but few stay when it is hard. He asks the reader to be a friend who remains in good times and in difficult ones.
The last chapter of Book Two is called the royal road of the holy cross. Thomas says that no one can escape suffering, but love and patience can make it lighter to carry.
Book Three is written like a conversation between Christ and a disciple. The disciple begins with the words of a psalm, asking to hear what God will say within him.
In this chapter, Thomas says that truth speaks without any noise of words. A teacher who speaks inside the heart, he writes, can teach us more than any noisy argument.
Thomas calls love a great thing, because it makes every heavy burden feel light. Love, he says, is quick and joyful, and it does not grow tired.
In the sixth chapter Thomas describes the signs of a person who truly loves God. Such a person is faithful and patient, does not seek only his own advantage and is not easily turned aside.
Thomas teaches that we should think modestly of ourselves when we stand before God. In his view, God's gifts flow most easily to those who do not demand them.
Thomas admits that the fight against our own bad desires is never finished. He asks for patience, because each small victory makes the next one a little easier.
Thomas advises the disciple to place all his cares in God's hands. This does not mean that we stop working, but that we stop being crushed by worry.

Thomas asks the disciple to bear insults and injuries with patience, following the example of Christ. Real patience, he says, is shown not when everything is pleasant, but when someone has wronged us.

In the twenty-third chapter Thomas names four things that bring great peace, such as choosing less rather than more. He also advises us to take the lowest place and to wish that God's will be done in us.
Thomas teaches that a heart is firmly at peace when it rests in God and not in the opinions of others. Such a heart is like a house on a rock, because it is not easily shaken.
Thomas praises a free mind, which stands above ordinary worries without despising people. He says that such freedom is not won in a day, but grows through steady prayer and humble work.
Thomas tells the disciple not to be troubled when people speak badly of him. Their words, he says, cannot change what he truly is before God.
Thomas advises the disciple to arrange his outward affairs wisely, and not to be too eager about worldly business. A person who runs after every task, he says, soon loses his inner calm.
In chapter forty-three of Book Three, Thomas warns the disciple against vain and worldly knowledge. Learning is not wrong, but a mind that only collects facts may miss the one thing that matters.
Thomas often turns his eyes to eternal life, and he asks the disciple to bear present troubles in that hope. In chapters forty-seven to forty-nine he writes about it with great longing.
There are times when a person feels dry, alone and discouraged, and Thomas does not hide this. He advises the disciple to stay humble and patient, and to trust that the dark time will pass.
In chapter fifty-seven, Thomas says that a person should not be too downcast when he falls into some fault. Even then, he writes, God asks us to rise gently and to begin again.

The last chapter of Book Three, number fifty-nine, asks the disciple to fix all his hope and trust in God alone. The chapter itself is a prayer of trust, in which the disciple offers his whole life to God.
Book Four is called a devout invitation to Holy Communion, the sacred meal that many Christians share. It begins with words of Christ, who invites all who are tired and troubled to come to him.

Thomas asks the believer to come to Communion with deep respect, because for Christians this is a holy mystery. He reminds us that no one is ever fully worthy, and that humility matters more than perfection.
Thomas teaches that a person should look honestly at his life before receiving Communion. He asks for sorrow for faults, a wish to do better and a heart that forgives others.
In the chapters on offering, the disciple gives everything he has to God, including his hopes, his work and his weaknesses. Thomas pictures this as a free gift, made out of love and not out of fear.
Thomas writes with longing to be close to God, and he calls it a union of the heart. He asks the reader to come with simple trust and not to be troubled by questions that cannot be answered.
Looking back over the four books, we can see clearly what they ask of the reader. They ask for a life that is humble, patient, honest within and loving toward others.
Soon after it was written, the book was copied by hand and passed from one monastery to the next. After the printing press arrived, it was printed many times and translated into many languages.
The Imitation of Christ does not ask us to be perfect today, only to begin. Choose one small act of humility or kindness, and let it be the first step on the road.
C1C2: Thomas à Kempis, born around 1380, spent most of his long life as a monk at a quiet monastery near the Dutch town of Zwolle. Tradition credits him with writing, in Latin and in the early fifteenth century, a small book of guidance for anyone who longs to follow Christ with an undivided heart. It became one of the most widely read Christian books in history, although its first readers were simply fellow monks.

The work is divided into four short books, each made of brief chapters that read more like quiet conversations than like a lecture. Its first words recall a line from the Gospel, in which Christ promises that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness. Everything that follows is an attempt to explain what such following means for the mind, the habits and the heart of an ordinary person.

Book One opens with a simple challenge, which is that a person should try to follow Christ rather than merely to admire him. Thomas observes that someone may know a great many sayings and still miss the spirit behind them, as a traveller might memorise a map without taking a single step. The first lesson of the book, therefore, is that the road is walked with the heart and the hands, not only with the mind.

What use is it, Thomas asks, to speak cleverly about great mysteries if one lacks the humility that makes them pleasing to God? He prefers a plain farmer who serves God faithfully to a proud scholar who can name every star but neglects his own soul. Learning is not condemned, yet the book insists that it must never become a way of feeling superior to other people.

Thomas urges his readers to hold a modest opinion of themselves, not from false shyness, but because honest self-knowledge shows how much each of us still has to learn. A person who sees his own failings clearly, he suggests, soon loses the appetite for judging everyone else. Humility in this book is therefore not a sad feeling, but a clear and truthful look in the mirror.

On the day of judgment, Thomas writes, we will not be asked how much we have read but how well we have lived. The sentence turns every page of the book into a quiet question, for it asks whether our knowledge has made us any kinder, braver or more patient. A single honest act of mercy, he implies, outweighs a library of fine arguments.

In the fifth chapter, Thomas advises readers to approach the Scriptures for the sake of the truth they contain and not for the elegance of their language. Each passage, he says, should be read in the same humble spirit in which it was first spoken, with a mind ready to be changed rather than a mind hunting for arguments. Reading of this kind becomes less like study and more like a patient act of listening, undertaken in silence and with an open heart.

Whenever a person desires something too strongly, Thomas observes, the heart at once becomes restless, like a field disturbed by wind. The proud and the greedy never find rest, while those who are poor in spirit live in the fullness of peace. The book therefore invites us to examine our wants, and to ask which of them we truly need.

Thomas cautions his readers against placing their hope in the favour of powerful people, in the size of their wealth or in the praise of the crowd. All of these, he says, are like houses built on sand, lovely to look at but unable to bear the weight of a whole life. The only dependable foundation, in his view, is a trust in God that does not rise and fall with the world's opinion.

Idle talk, Thomas observes, is one of the easiest ways of losing peace, since people so often leave a long conversation emptier and more restless than when they entered it. He therefore advises his readers to speak less, to keep their words for what is useful and kind, and to enjoy the silence that follows. It is a surprisingly modern lesson for a restless world in which almost nobody ever seems to stop talking.

Thomas insists that a little trouble, wisely received, can do a person good, since hardship reminds us that we are not in command of everything. It shows us who we are when comfort is taken away, and it teaches patience and a quieter kind of courage. Those who have never been tested, he implies, hardly know what they are made of.

No one in this life, Thomas teaches, is wholly free from temptation, and even the most saintly people have had to struggle with it. The best time to resist is at the very beginning, when a wrong thought first knocks at the door of the mind, for a small seed is easier to pull up than a full-grown tree. Seen this way, temptation is not a sign of failure but a place where strength can grow.

It is easy to pass judgment on other people, Thomas says, yet we seldom know the whole truth of their circumstances or the secret struggles in their hearts. He therefore turns our attention back to our own faults, which are the only ones we are truly able to correct. Gentleness towards other people, in the view of this book, always begins with a thoroughly honest look at ourselves.

If we are unable to make ourselves into the people we long to be, Thomas asks, how can we expect others to become exactly what we would like them to be? We are often quick to correct another person, yet slow to notice that we too need correction and patience. The remedy he proposes is to bear one another's faults gently, knowing that each of us carries a burden that others cannot see.

Thomas loved solitude and silence, believing that a person who withdraws from noise, even for a short time, begins to hear what is happening within. In the same part of the book he offers a well-known thought, that we may make our plans but the final outcome lies beyond our power. Together, these ideas teach a kind of restful modesty, in which effort is honest and the result is gently left in other hands.

Thomas does not hide from the fact of death, and in a short and solemn chapter he asks his readers to keep it quietly in mind. Life is shorter than we imagine, he says, and so each morning ought to be treated as though it might be the last. The purpose of the thought is not to frighten, but to clear away trivial worries and to bring our attention to what truly matters.

Book One closes with an urgent but kindly appeal, which is that we should begin to improve our lives at once. Thomas does not expect sudden perfection, for he knows how slowly a heart changes, but he asks for daily effort, however small, and for a firm decision to keep trying. A habit begun today, however humble, is worth more than a grand plan left for tomorrow.

Book Two takes as its starting point a line from the Gospel of Luke, that the kingdom of God is within you, and it turns that line into a whole way of life. Thomas invites readers to look less at outward circumstances and more at the quiet room of the heart, where peace is either welcomed or turned away. He suggests that the traveller who learns to live within no longer needs to run after every passing comfort.

A peaceful person, Thomas says, does more good than a person who is merely learned, because calm is a form of generosity that others can feel at once. Keep yourself first in peace, he advises, and then you will be able to bring peace to those around you. A quarrelsome heart spreads its trouble like smoke, but a settled heart quietly clears the air.

With a charming image, Thomas says that a person is lifted above the things of this world by two wings, which are simplicity and purity. Simplicity belongs to our intention, he explains, since it asks us to aim at one honest goal, while purity belongs to our affection, since it asks us to love without selfish mixture. A heart equipped with both, the image suggests, could rise as easily as a bird leaves the ground.

The truest glory, Thomas writes, is the joy of a good conscience, and he calls it the one happiness that neither flattery nor insult can touch. People may praise us, but praise cannot make us better than we are, and blame cannot make us worse. A person who lives honestly can therefore sleep soundly, whatever the neighbours may say.

For Thomas, the heart of the Christian life is a close friendship with Jesus, whom he asks his readers to love above all other things. Earthly friends are precious, he admits, but they change, grow tired or are taken from us, whereas this friend remains when every other has gone. To keep him near, he says, one must be humble and quiet, and ready to listen.

Thomas makes a sober observation in the eleventh chapter, which is that many people are glad to follow Jesus while life is easy, but only a few remain when it becomes hard. Plenty of people want his comforts, he says, but few are willing to carry any share of his cross. The challenge he leaves is whether our love can survive when it costs us something.

Book Two ends with what Thomas calls the royal road of the holy cross, a way that every Christian must walk in one form or another. Suffering cannot be avoided in this life, he teaches, wherever we run, but love and patience can change the way it is carried. Those who go forward willingly, he promises, find that the burden, which seemed unbearable from a distance, grows lighter with every step.

Book Three changes its form and becomes a conversation between Christ and a disciple, in which the two voices answer one another like prayer and reply. It opens with a line from the Psalms, where the disciple says that he wishes to hear what the Lord will speak within his heart. The longest and warmest part of the whole work follows, as if the reader had been invited to overhear a private talk.

In the second chapter the disciple asks to be taught by truth itself, which speaks without any noise of words and without the confusion of rival opinions. Many voices around us are loud and quick to persuade, but the voice he seeks is gentle, and it is heard only when the mind has grown quiet. Wisdom of this kind, Thomas suggests, is received as a gift by a patient listener rather than manufactured by clever effort.

Love, Thomas exclaims in the fifth chapter, is a great thing, for it makes every heavy burden light and bears the whole of a hard road without complaint. It runs, it flies, it rejoices, and it is not easily discouraged, because it looks to a goal beyond itself. A heart on fire with this love, he suggests, will do gladly what duty alone could only do with a groan.

In the sixth chapter Thomas draws a portrait of a true lover of God, and the portrait is surprisingly steady rather than dramatic. Such a person is faithful through trouble, patient with delay and glad to serve without seeking any private reward. He is not easily turned aside from his purpose, whether by flattery, by fear or by the slow wearing down of the years.

Thomas teaches that the disciple should think little of himself in the sight of God, not from gloom but from the plain recognition of how much he has received. Grace, in his picture, behaves like water, which runs down to the low places and leaves the high ones dry. The humble person is therefore the one who is truly ready, because a hand that is already full cannot take what is offered.

In the twelfth chapter of this book Thomas does not pretend that the struggle against our own wrong desires is quickly won. He asks his readers to be patient with themselves, to fight again each day, and to expect that every small victory will make the next one a little less hard. The idea is deeply practical, for it treats character as something built by many modest decisions rather than by a single heroic leap.

In the seventeenth chapter the voice of Christ invites the disciple to cast every anxiety upon God and to trust that it will be well looked after. This does not mean idleness, for the same book praises honest work, but it does mean that we no longer carry each trouble as though its outcome depended on us alone. Those who learn to release their fears in this way, Thomas implies, find that the weight on their shoulders grows lighter.

Thomas turns to the question of how we should respond when others insult or injure us, and he points to the example of Christ, who bore far worse without bitterness. Real patience, he says, is not proved when everything is pleasant and people are kind, but when someone has wronged us and we choose not to answer in kind. This is among the hardest teachings of the book, and Thomas does not pretend otherwise.

In the twenty-third chapter Thomas names four things that bring great peace, among them to choose less rather than more and to seek the lowest place. Each of them goes against the grain of our natural ambition, yet each one, he says, lays down some heavy load from the shoulders. The person who practises them may look quiet from outside, but within there is a settled calm that the loudest success never gives.

Firm peace of heart, Thomas explains, does not come from having everything arranged to our liking, because the world is never so obliging. It comes from resting in God and from loving what is truly good, and a heart so settled is like a house built on rock, which storms may strike but cannot shift. Such calm is not the absence of trouble, but the presence of something steadier than trouble.

In chapter twenty-six the disciple prays for what Thomas calls a free mind, one that stands above the small anxieties of daily life without looking down on anyone. Such freedom is not seized in a single day, he cautions, but grows slowly through steady prayer, honest reading and quiet attention. The result, when it comes, is a lightness of spirit that no change of fortune can fully remove.

Thomas has the voice of Christ say, in chapter thirty-six, that his follower should fix his heart on God and not fear the judgment of men. A wounding word, or even a false rumour, can pass over us like a breeze, for it cannot alter what we truly are in the sight of God. Praise, too, should be received lightly, since the same people who applaud today may forget us tomorrow.

Thomas is not an enemy of practical life, and in chapters thirty-eight and thirty-nine he advises the disciple to arrange his outward affairs sensibly and to turn everything to God. What he fears is the feverish hurry of someone who chases every task and every success, for such a person soon loses his inner calm. Work done in peace, he suggests, is better work, and it leaves a person more of himself at the end of the day.

In chapter forty-three Thomas warns the disciple against vain and worldly knowledge, the kind that fills the head but leaves the heart exactly as it was. Learning in itself is not wrong, he allows, yet a mind that only collects facts may miss the quiet wisdom that makes a person gentle and honest. The true teacher, in his view, is the one who leads us from clever talk to quiet love.

Near the end of Book Three, Thomas turns his eyes more and more towards eternal life, and he asks the disciple to endure present troubles in the light of that hope. In chapters forty-seven to forty-nine he writes of that day with a quiet longing, as a traveller might speak of a home he has not yet reached. For a Christian reader, the thought gives hardship a horizon, so that each difficulty is seen as one stage on a longer road.

Thomas knows that there are seasons when a person feels dry, abandoned or discouraged, and in chapter fifty he speaks of them honestly. He advises the disciple to remain humble and patient, to keep doing the small tasks that are within reach, and to trust that the dark time will not last for ever. It is a comforting passage for anyone who has ever wondered why an effort to live well can sometimes feel so empty.

In chapter fifty-seven Thomas says that a person should not be too downcast when he falls into some fault, because despair is a greater danger than the fall itself. A child who stumbles is not scolded for ever, and neither, he suggests, is the heart that has stumbled and wishes to do better. The wise response is to rise gently, say sorry, and begin the road again with a little more care.

The longest book comes to a close with chapter fifty-nine, in which the disciple fixes all his hope and trust in God alone. The chapter is itself a prayer, a calm and grateful offering of a whole life, with its weakness and its worries, into hands that are stronger than his own. After so many pages of advice, the book ends its central section not with a rule but with an act of trust.

Book Four is a devout invitation to Holy Communion, the sacred meal that many Christians share in remembrance of Christ, and it is written for those who receive it in faith. It begins with words from the Gospel of Matthew in which Christ calls to everyone who is tired and troubled, promising to give them rest. Readers from other traditions may simply notice how much of the book is about preparing the heart before approaching something holy.

Thomas asks the believer to approach Communion with deep reverence, since for Christians this is one of the holiest acts of their faith. He is clear that no one is ever perfectly worthy of it, and that what is wanted is a humble and sincere heart rather than a spotless record. The tone of these chapters is awe rather than fear, as of someone entering a very large and quiet room.

Before receiving Communion, Thomas teaches, a person should look honestly at his own life, admit his faults and ask for the strength to amend them. He asks for sorrow without despair, a wish to do better and a heart that has forgiven others in turn. In this way the practice of the sacrament and the practice of daily kindness are bound firmly together.

Book Four also speaks of offering, and the disciple presents to God everything he has, including his hopes, his work and even his weaknesses. Thomas pictures this as a gift made freely and out of love, not as a payment demanded out of fear. What remains in the end, he suggests, is a heart that has stopped holding tightly to itself and has found a quiet joy in giving.

As Book Four moves on, Thomas writes with growing longing for closeness to God, which he describes as a union of the heart and not merely of the mind. Near the end he warns against curious and restless questioning of this mystery, and asks the reader to approach in simple faith, as a child accepts a gift. It is a reminder that, for Thomas, the deepest things are received with open hands rather than seized by argument.

Looking back over the four books, we can see how closely their themes belong together, for each one returns to humility, patience, inner honesty and love. Thomas does not offer a system or a set of clever arguments, but a series of gentle invitations to look inward and to begin again. Whether or not a reader shares his faith, the steady, practical kindness of his advice is easy to recognise.

Soon after it was written, the little book was copied by hand and carried from one monastery to another, and after the invention of printing it appeared in edition after edition. It has since been translated into a great many languages, and it is often counted among the most widely read Christian books after the Bible. Its readers have come from many backgrounds and centuries, drawn by the plain and heartfelt voice that speaks quietly from its pages.

The Imitation of Christ is a book to be lived rather than finished, and its quiet advice is meant to be tried one small act at a time. Choose a single practice, whether it is silence, patience or a kind word to someone who finds you difficult, and carry it through the day. For its readers over the centuries, this is how the imitation of Christ has always begun, not with a great vow, but with an ordinary morning and an honest heart.
